A LocalScript plays a sword-swing animation when the player clicks:
```lua
local humanoid = player.Character:WaitForChild("Humanoid")
tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    local track = humanoid:LoadAnimation(script.SwingAnim)
    track:Play()
end)
```
The animation was exported from the Animation Editor with its priority left at Core. In game the swing is barely visible: while standing or walking the arms keep following the default idle/walk animation. Explain why and fix it.
answer_key: Cause: Core is the lowest AnimationPriority; the default Animate script's idle/walk tracks have a higher priority, and when tracks animate the same joints the highest-priority track wins (same-priority tracks are blended by weight), so idle/walk override the swing
Fix: give the swing a higher priority such as Action (or Action2-Action4), either re-exported from the Animation Editor or by setting track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action before Play()

Load the animation through the Animator (humanoid:FindFirstChildOfClass("Animator"):LoadAnimation) instead of the deprecated Humanoid:LoadAnimation, and load the track once and reuse it instead of creating a new track on every click

The default Animate script plays idle/walk at Idle/Movement priority, so on any joint both animate, the higher priority wins and your swing loses on the arms. Fix: make it Action (re-export with priority Action in the Animation Editor, or set it in code). Also load the track once through the Animator, not Humanoid:LoadAnimation (deprecated) on every click, which keeps creating tracks.

local char = player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()
local animator = char:WaitForChild('Humanoid'):WaitForChild('Animator')
local track = animator:LoadAnimation(script.SwingAnim)
track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action
tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    if not track.IsPlaying then track:Play(0.05) end
end)

prompt: A shop ScrollingFrame contains a UIListLayout. Item buttons are cloned into it at runtime from a config (sometimes 8 items, sometimes 40). CanvasSize was set in Studio to {0, 0}, {0, 600}. With many items the player cannot scroll down to the last ones. What is wrong and what is the cleanest fix?
answer_key: CanvasSize defines the scrollable area and is fixed; it does not grow when children are added, so content beyond 600 px is unreachable
Fix: set AutomaticCanvasSize to Y (Enum.AutomaticSize.Y) and leave the CanvasSize Y at 0, or update CanvasSize from the UIListLayout's AbsoluteContentSize (listening for it to change)

Cleanest fix: set ScrollingFrame.AutomaticCanvasSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.Y and CanvasSize = UDim2.new(0,0,0,0), and let the engine size the canvas from the content. Alternative: update from the layout, e.g. `list:GetPropertyChangedSignal("AbsoluteContentSize"):Connect(function() sf.CanvasSize = UDim2.fromOffset(0, list.AbsoluteContentSize.Y + padding) end)`.
Also: give the items a fixed offset height (or a UIAspectRatioConstraint), not a Y scale relative to the canvas, because scale-Y children and automatic canvas feed back into each other. Account for UIPadding, and set ScrollingDirection = Y.

prompt: A hover platform (one unanchored 20x2x20 stud part) has an Attachment at one corner and a VectorForce using that attachment as Attachment0 with Force = Vector3.new(0, 5000, 0). The platform never lifts off. After the developer raised the force a lot, it rises but as soon as it tilts it starts sliding and spinning away sideways. Explain the problems and how to set the VectorForce up correctly.
answer_key: To lift, the upward force must exceed the weight = assembly mass x workspace.Gravity (default 196.2 studs/s^2); compute it from AssemblyMass (or GetMass for a single part) instead of guessing a constant like 5000

RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force is expressed in the attachment's frame and tilts with the part, pushing it sideways; set RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World for a constant upward force

By default the force is applied at Attachment0's position (ApplyAtCenterOfMass = false); an off-centre attachment creates torque that spins the platform, so enable ApplyAtCenterOfMass (or centre the attachment) and keep it level with something like an AlignOrientation

responses.R1: 1) Too little force: weight = AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity. A 20x2x20 plastic part is 800 studs^3 * 0.7 = 560 mass units; with gravity 196.2 that needs ~110,000 force just to hover, so 5000 does nothing. 2) Force is applied at a corner attachment, so it also creates torque and tips the part. 3) RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force is in the attachment's local frame; once tilted the 'up' vector points sideways and pushes the platform away, which tilts it more (runaway sliding/spinning). Correct setup: put the attachment at the center of mass (or set ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true), set RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World, Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity, 0) (recompute if mass changes; add a small extra or a PD term to rise/hold height). Add an AlignOrientation (or AngularVelocity/damping) to keep it level, and for height-holding prefer AlignPosition or a controller rather than a raw constant force.
responses.R2:
Problems:
1) 5000 is less than the platform's weight. Lift needs Force.Y > AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity (196.2 studs/s^2). A 20x2x20 plastic part (density 0.7) is 800 stud^3, mass ~560, weight ~110,000.
2) Force is applied at the corner attachment (ApplyAtCenterOfMass = false), producing torque, so it tilts.
3) RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force rotates with the part: once tilted, 'up' points sideways and it slides and spins away.
Correct setup:
```lua
local att = Instance.new("Attachment", platform) -- at center
local vf = Instance.new("VectorForce")
vf.Attachment0 = att
vf.ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true
vf.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World
vf.Force = Vector3.new(0, platform.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity, 0) -- exact hover; add extra to rise
vf.Parent = platform
```
Add AlignOrientation (PrimaryAxisParallel to world up) to keep it level, and for controlled height/speed use AlignPosition or LinearVelocity; a constant net force accelerates forever. Recompute if mass changes; anchored parts ignore it.
responses.R3:
Problems:
1) Too little force: 5000 is below the weight. Lift needs Force >= AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity (gravity defaults to 196.2). A 20x2x20 plastic part (~800 stud^3 at density 0.7) weighs about 560 mass * 196.2 = ~110,000.
2) Off-center application: the force acts at the corner Attachment0, so it also creates a torque and the platform tips.
3) RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force rotates with the part. Once it tilts, the "up" force gains a sideways part and pushes it to slide and spin.
Correct setup: put the attachment at the center (or set ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true), and set RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World with Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity * k, 0) (k slightly above 1 to rise, 1 to hover). A constant VectorForce has no speed cap and no height control, so add damping or a controller, or use AlignPosition/LinearVelocity for height. Add AlignOrientation (OneAttachment, PrimaryAxisParallel to world up) to keep it level. Give the server network ownership, or anchor while idle.

Compute the force: part:GetMass() * workspace.Gravity (sum the mass of the whole assembly) plus whatever extra lift you want. 2) Off-centre attachment: a force applied at a corner creates torque, so the platform tips. 3) RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, so the force is in the attachment's local frame. answer_key: The sessions table is keyed by Player and never cleared, so players (and their data) stay referenced after leaving; remove the entry in Players.PlayerRemoving

A new RunService.Heartbeat connection is made for every character and never disconnected; it keeps running and keeps the old character alive after death/respawn. Store the connection and Disconnect it when the character dies or is removed (or use a cleanup/maid pattern, Destroying event)

Destroy() disconnects all connections on an instance and its descendants, but old characters / Player objects are not guaranteed to be destroyed by default; enable Workspace.PlayerCharacterDestroyBehavior (Enabled) or explicitly Destroy old characters so their own connections are released

responses.R1:
Leaks:
1) sessions[player] is never removed. The table holds strong refs to Player objects and their growing history tables.
2) Each CharacterAdded makes a new Heartbeat connection that is never disconnected. After every respawn the old connections keep running on dead characters (and keep them in memory), so N respawns means N updaters per player.
3) The CharacterAdded connection itself, and the history tables if they grow without a cap.
Fix:
```lua
local conns = {}
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    sessions[player] = { kills = 0, history = {} }
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(char)
        if conns[player] then conns[player]:Disconnect() end
        conns[player] = RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function()
            if char.Parent then updateAura(char) end
        end)
        char.Destroying:Connect(function() -- or Humanoid.Died
            if conns[player] then conns[player]:Disconnect(); conns[player] = nil end
        end)
    end)
end)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    if conns[player] then conns[player]:Disconnect(); conns[player] = nil end
    sessions[player] = nil
end)
```
Better: run one Heartbeat loop that iterates the active characters instead of one per player. Cap history (a ring buffer), set workspace.PlayerCharacterDestroyBehavior to Enabled, and check memory with the Dev Console Memory/LuaHeap view.

2) Each CharacterAdded makes a new Heartbeat connection that is never disconnected. Each respawn adds another one that keeps running updateAura on dead characters and keeps them referenced. Heartbeat is long-lived, so destroying the character doesn't disconnect it.
3) Unbounded history growth: cap it (ring buffer).
Fix:

```lua
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    local s = { kills = 0, history = {}, conns = {} }
    sessions[player] = s
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(char)

            if s.aura then s.aura:Disconnect(); s.aura = nil end
        end)
    end)
end)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    local s = sessions[player]
    if s and s.aura then s.aura:Disconnect() end
    sessions[player] = nil
end)
```

prompt: A game has drivable cars (VehicleSeat + constraints) and server-controlled NPC guards that chase players. Cars feel laggy for drivers, and exploiters sometimes fling guards or teleport cars. Describe how network ownership should be set up for each and what the security implications are.
answer_key: The engine auto-assigns ownership of unanchored parts to nearby clients; for a car, call SetNetworkOwner(driver) when someone sits in the seat and SetNetworkOwnershipAuto() (or nil) when the seat is vacated, so the driver simulates it with no input lag

Gameplay-critical NPCs can be kept server-owned with SetNetworkOwner(nil) (sparingly, since it can look jittery to clients); ownership applies to the whole assembly/mechanism, and anchored parts cannot have their owner set

Roblox cannot verify physics from a client that owns a part (it can move it anywhere and fake Touched), so the server must validate client-owned results (speed/position sanity checks) or use Server Authority mode

responses.R1:
Cars: give the driver network ownership of the whole vehicle assembly (VehicleSeat does this automatically when a player sits, or call SetNetworkOwner(driver) on the chassis root on the server when the Occupant changes). The driver then simulates locally with no input lag. Return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or auto when they leave. Never anchor parts mid-drive, because anchored parts are always server-owned.
NPC guards: SetNetworkOwner(nil) on the HumanoidRootPart (or every part) after spawning, so ownership never ping-pongs to nearby players. That stops jitter, and players can't move them.
Security: whoever owns an assembly is trusted for its physics. Exploiters can teleport or fling anything they own, including their car and anything it touches. Physics contacts between client-owned and server parts can still be abused, so the server must validate car speed and position deltas, distances, and damage or kill events, not trust them. With auto ownership a guard can end up owned by an exploiter, which is why guards are server-owned. For a competitive game consider Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server (2026 Server Authority), which makes the server authoritative with client prediction instead of trusting owners.

The client simulates the physics, so steering has no round-trip lag. Set it back to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil) or automatic) when the driver leaves. Security: the owning client controls that assembly's physics, so an exploiter can teleport or fling their car. The server must sanity-check it on Heartbeat (speed and position deltas against a cap, no-clip/teleport distance) and correct or kick. Don't let car collisions apply authoritative damage to others without server checks. NPC guards: call SetNetworkOwner(nil) on every guard's parts (after they're parented and unanchored) so the server always owns them. Otherwise, automatic ownership hands them to nearby players, which causes the flinging: an exploiter who owns the guard's physics can move or fling it. Pathfinding, damage and AI live on the server. prompt: A bad update yesterday corrupted some players' save data in a standard (non-ordered) DataStore. Design a support tool that restores a given player's data to what it was just before the update. What does the engine keep, which APIs do you use, and what are the limits?
answer_key: Standard data stores keep versioned backups automatically: a backup version is created on the first write to each key in each UTC hour (later writes in that hour overwrite it), and backups expire 30 days after being overwritten (the latest version never expires)

Find the version with DataStore:ListVersionsAsync(key, sortDirection, minDate, maxDate) and read it with GetVersionAsync(key, version) or GetVersionAtTimeAsync(key, timestampMs); then write it back with SetAsync/UpdateAsync while the player is not in a session that would overwrite it
The same can be done from outside the game with the Open Cloud data stores API using an API key limited to that experience/data store (entry list/read/update permissions, optional IP restriction)

responses.R1: Standard DataStores are versioned automatically. Each SetAsync/UpdateAsync/IncrementAsync/RemoveAsync creates a version (with VersionId and CreatedTime), and old versions are kept for 30 days (writes close together may be merged into hourly snapshots). Tool design: (1) an admin-only command or Open Cloud script takes a userId and the update timestamp. (2) Call store:GetVersionAtTimeAsync(key, updateTimeMillis) to get the last version before the update, or ListVersionsAsync(key, Enum.SortDirection.Descending, minDate, maxDate, pageSize) followed by GetVersionAsync(key, versionId). (3) Inspect or validate the data, then write it back with UpdateAsync/SetAsync, which creates a new version, so a bad restore can itself be rolled back. (4) Make sure the player is not online, or release or take over the session lock, so a live server does not overwrite the restore. Kick the player or use a MemoryStore/MessagingService signal. prompt: A team wants a web admin panel (outside Roblox) that can (1) push an announcement to every live server instantly and (2) grant an item to a specific player, who may be online or offline. Design this.
answer_key: Use Open Cloud with an API key created on the Creator Hub, scoped to the experience and only the needed permissions (messaging publish, data store entries), sent in the x-api-key header from the backend; never ship the key to clients; optional IP restriction/expiry

Live servers: POST to the Open Cloud messaging endpoint (universes/{universeId}:publishMessage) with a topic and message; each server subscribes with MessagingService:SubscribeAsync(topic, callback) and reads message.Data

Messaging delivery is best effort and not guaranteed (messages up to ~1 KB), so durable grants are written to a data store (via Open Cloud) as a pending grant that the server applies on join or when notified
Open Cloud publishing shares the MessagingService rate limits of the experience, so the panel must respect those limits (batch/throttle announcements)

responses.R1:
Architecture: web panel -> your backend (holds Open Cloud API keys in a secret manager, with auth and audit log) -> Roblox Open Cloud.
(1) Announcements: backend calls the Open Cloud MessagingService publish endpoint (universe messaging, e.g. topic "Announce"). Each server subscribes with MessagingService:SubscribeAsync("Announce") and shows the text to its players through a RemoteEvent. Limits: 1 KB message, best-effort delivery (~1-2 s, no ordering or guarantee). Include an id so servers ignore duplicates. Optionally also write the announcement to a DataStore/MemoryStore so servers that start late can read it.
(2) Grants: don't edit live profiles directly. Write a pending grant to a "PendingGrants" key/queue for the userId through Open Cloud DataStore (v2 entries API) or a MemoryStore queue, with a unique grantId. Then publish a "grant" message. The server that has the player online (or the next server they join, on load) claims the grant atomically with UpdateAsync, applies it to the profile, and marks the grantId as consumed (idempotent, so no double grants). Editing an offline player's main key directly from Open Cloud is risky because there is no UpdateAsync transform and it can race a live session.
Security: one API key per purpose with minimal scopes (messaging publish; datastore read/update on specific stores), restricted to the experience, with expiry and rotation. Honor 429/retry-after with backoff. Open Cloud writes share the experience's DataStore budget. Validate item ids server-side.
responses.R2: (1) Announcements: the panel backend calls the Open Cloud MessagingService API (POST .../universes/{universeId}/topics/{topic}:publish, API key with messaging-service:publish scope). Every server does MessagingService:SubscribeAsync('Announcements', ...) and shows the message (validate/size-limit text, max 1 KB, best-effort delivery). (2) Item grants: write the grant durably first, then notify. Backend writes to the player's 'pending grants' (Open Cloud DataStore entry like Grants_<userId>, or a MemoryStore queue/sorted map for short-lived) with a unique grantId. Then it publishes a MessagingService message 'grant' with the userId. The server that has the player online consumes it: UpdateAsync on the pending key to atomically remove the grant, add the item to the player's session data and save. Offline players: on join, the server checks the pending key and applies it. Don't let the panel write directly into the live player-data key, because the online server's session would overwrite it. Use idempotency (track applied grantIds) so retries/duplicate messages don't double-grant. Security: API keys stored server-side only, least-privilege scopes limited to this universe, IP allowlist and expiry, panel auth + audit log; Roblox servers treat messages as commands only from the trusted topic and validate payloads.

prompt: A developer splits server code into many Scripts that talk through BindableEvents, passing state tables like `{player = plr, inventory = invObject}` where invObject is a table with a metatable (OOP class). Methods on the received object fail. Explain what goes wrong and how ModuleScripts would change the design.
answer_key: BindableEvent/BindableFunction arguments are copied, not passed by reference: tables lose identity and their metatable (so OOP methods disappear), mixed array/dictionary tables can lose elements, and non-string keys are converted to strings; bindables also only work on the same side of the client-server boundary

A ModuleScript runs once per Luau environment and require() returns the same cached value to every server script, so systems can share live objects/state by requiring each other (client and server get separate copies)
BindableFunction:Invoke yields until a callback handles it (never resumes if none is set), and cyclic requires between modules hang rather than error, so dependencies should be one-directional

responses.R1: BindableEvent/BindableFunction arguments are serialized and copied across the call, like remotes: tables are deep-copied, metatables are stripped, functions are dropped, mixed/non-string keys can be lost, and Instances pass by reference. So the receiver gets a plain data table without the class metatable, so methods like inv:AddItem() are nil, and changes made to the copy don't affect the original object (two diverging states). Also identity checks fail (copy ~= original). ModuleScripts fix this: require() returns the same cached table to every Script in the same environment (server vs client), so you share real objects and call functions directly with no serialization. Typical design: one or a few Scripts as entry points, the rest as service modules (InventoryService, CombatService) that expose functions like InventoryService.get(player) returning the live OOP object; modules communicate through direct calls or a custom signal module (pure Luau signal that passes values by reference). Benefits: type checking/autocomplete, explicit dependencies, no timing races of BindableEvents firing before listeners connect. Keep Bindables only where you need decoupled cross-environment or Instance-based events, and pass ids/data instead of objects there.
responses.R2: Bindable (and Remote) events serialize arguments by deep copy: tables arrive as new tables and metatables are stripped, so invObject arrives as a plain table with no methods (inv:Add() errors with "attempt to call a nil value"). Functions aren't passed, keys may change (mixed/non-string keys are dropped or converted), and identity is lost. Mutations on the receiver don't affect the sender's copy, so state goes out of sync. Instances like the Player pass by reference. ModuleScripts: require returns the same cached table to every Script in the same VM/context, so put the inventory service in a ModuleScript (InventoryService.get(player) returns the actual object with its metatable). Other scripts call methods directly, share one source of truth, get typed APIs, and need no serialization. The usual design is a single Script entry point (bootstrap) that requires service modules, with Signal-style module events instead of BindableEvents for internal communication. Keep BindableEvents only for loose fire-and-forget notifications that pass plain data or Instances.
responses.R3:
BindableEvents (like remotes) copy arguments across the boundary. Tables are deep-copied, and metatables are stripped, so invObject arrives as a plain table: method calls (obj:Add()) are nil, and mutations hit a copy, not the original state. Other limits: mixed or non-string keys are lost or converted, functions are dropped, and Instances are passed by reference (the player is fine). Each Fire also has cross-script overhead and deferred ordering.
ModuleScripts: require() returns the same table to every Script in the same VM context (cached per environment), so the scripts share real references. Make an InventoryService module that owns the state (inventories[player]) and exposes functions or class objects. Other server modules require it and call methods directly, with metatables intact and no copying. Keep one entry Script that requires the services (a single-script architecture), use plain function calls or module-level signals for events, and keep BindableEvents only for loose decoupling with plain data (ids, numbers), never live objects.
responses.R4: BindableEvent/BindableFunction arguments are serialized the same way as remotes. Tables are copied, metatables are dropped, functions are not transferred, and mixed or non-string keys can break. The receiver gets a plain data copy of invObject with no metatable, so invObject:AddItem() is nil and errors. Because it is a copy, mutations also never reach the original. Instances (player) do pass by reference. With ModuleScripts: require() runs a module once per VM and returns the same cached table to every script, so put InventoryService (the class plus a player -> inventory map) in a ModuleScript and have other systems require it and call methods directly on the real object. Real cross-system events become a Signal module (a pure Luau signal that passes values by reference) or callbacks, instead of Bindables. Most teams end up with one or a few entry Scripts that require service modules (single-script architecture), which gives explicit dependencies, typed APIs and shared state without serialization.

Metatables are stripped, so invObject arrives as a plain table without its class methods (inv:Add() is nil -> error). Functions are dropped, non-string keys become strings, mixed or sparse arrays can lose entries, and changes the receiver makes to its copy never reach the sender's object, so state drifts apart. (Instance references like the Player do survive.)
ModuleScripts fix this: require() runs a module once per Luau environment and returns the same cached table to every server script. A shared InventoryService module (e.g. InventoryService.get(player) returning the live OOP object) lets all systems call methods on the same object directly, with no copying, and with types/autocomplete. Use direct function calls or a pure-Luau Signal module for in-process events (those pass references and keep metatables), and keep BindableEvents for loose, primitive-only messages. Structure: a few Scripts that bootstrap service modules, with services requiring each other. Note that server and client get separate module copies, so cross-boundary communication still needs remotes.

prompt: To show other players' aim direction and footstep VFX, a client fires a RemoteEvent 30 times per second, and the server re-broadcasts to all clients. Under load, remote queues back up and important events (hits, purchases) arrive late. Someone suggests UnreliableRemoteEvent. Explain when it is appropriate and its constraints.
answer_key: UnreliableRemoteEvent does not resend lost events and does not guarantee order, so it fits ephemeral/continuously refreshed cosmetic data (aim direction, VFX) but not state that must arrive (hits, purchases, inventory), which stays on RemoteEvent
Payloads larger than 1000 bytes are dropped (silently in live games; Studio Output reports it), so send compact data such as numbers/ids rather than large tables
It has the same trust model as RemoteEvent: the server must still validate and rate-limit what clients send before re-broadcasting

responses.R1:
UnreliableRemoteEvent is right for high-frequency, cosmetic, superseded-by-the-next-update data: aim/look direction, footstep VFX, cheap visual positions. Losing or reordering one packet doesn't matter because the next one replaces it, and it doesn't clog the reliable queue, so hits and purchases stop being delayed.
Constraints: no delivery or ordering guarantee (include a sequence number/timestamp and drop stale ones). Payloads over ~1,000 bytes are dropped silently, so keep them tiny (e.g. compressed angles or buffers). Same API as RemoteEvent (FireServer/FireAllClients/OnServerEvent). Never use it for state that must arrive: hits, damage, purchases, ability start/stop, inventory. Still validate on server (types, NaN, magnitude, rate limit per player).
Also reduce the load: send 10-20 Hz instead of 30, only when changed, FireAllClients except sender or only to nearby players, and let clients derive footsteps locally from character movement instead of networking them.
responses.R2: UnreliableRemoteEvent is right for high-frequency, ephemeral and superseding data like aim direction, cosmetic positions and footstep VFX, where a lost or late packet doesn't matter because a newer one comes soon. It doesn't take up the reliable ordered queue, so hits and purchases on normal RemoteEvents stop waiting behind it. Constraints: delivery isn't guaranteed and there's no ordering, so include a timestamp or sequence and ignore stale packets. The payload must be 1,000 bytes or less or it is silently dropped; send compact values (e.g. a quantised yaw/pitch or a buffer), not big tables. Messages over the throttle are dropped rather than delayed, and messages are dropped if there's no connected handler. Never use it for state changes, damage, currency or purchases (keep those on reliable RemoteEvents with server validation). Still validate and rate-limit on the server. Also reduce the volume: send aim at about 10-20 Hz only when it changes, batch several players into one broadcast, let clients play footstep VFX locally from replicated character movement instead of networking them, and don't re-broadcast the event to the client that sent it.
responses.R3: UnreliableRemoteEvent is meant for high-frequency, ephemeral, cosmetic data where only the latest value matters: aim direction, look angles, footstep/VFX triggers. Messages are unordered and may be dropped (no resend), and they don't queue behind or block reliable traffic, so the reliable RemoteEvents (hits, purchases) are no longer delayed by them. Constraints: payload is small (about 1000 bytes per call; larger sends are dropped), so send compact data (e.g. a quantized Vector3 or buffer), never anything that must arrive or arrive in order (damage, purchases, state changes, start/stop pairs: use a reliable event or make each packet self-contained state); OnServerEvent/OnClientEvent API is the same; still validate and rate-limit on the server (exploiters can spam it), and type check. Also reduce load: lower the rate (10-20 Hz) and interpolate on receivers, send only on change, broadcast only to nearby players, and don't re-broadcast footsteps that other clients can derive from replicated animation/position.
responses.R4:
UnreliableRemoteEvent suits high-frequency, cosmetic, replaceable data where only the latest value matters: aim direction, look angles, footstep/VFX cues, positions of cheap objects. Dropping one is harmless because the next update replaces it. It doesn't wait for retransmits or ordering, so it doesn't block the reliable queue, and reliable events (hits, purchases) stop waiting behind the 30 Hz spam.
Constraints:
- Delivery is not guaranteed and order is not guaranteed. Add sequence numbers (with wraparound) and drop stale ones. Interpolate on the receiver.
- Payload limit is about 1,000 bytes (older docs said 900; design for under 900). Larger payloads are dropped, not split. Send compact data (e.g. a buffer or quantized angles).
- Throttled excess is dropped, not delayed.
- Never use it for state changes, ability start/stop, hits, damage or purchases. Those stay on RemoteEvent with server validation.
- The server still validates: check types, finite numbers (math.isfinite), unit-length vectors, and a per-player rate limit before re-broadcasting.
Also reduce volume: send at 10-20 Hz or only on change, use FireAllClients except the sender, or skip relaying and let clients derive footsteps locally from character movement.
responses.R5: UnreliableRemoteEvent suits high-frequency, ephemeral, latest-value-wins data where a dropped or out-of-order packet doesn't matter: aim direction, cosmetic footstep VFX, look angles. Constraints: no delivery or ordering guarantee (packets may drop under load). The payload must be small: about 1000 bytes max per call (around 900 usable), and larger calls are dropped. No return values (no unreliable function). Never use it for hits, damage, purchases, inventory or state transitions, which stay on reliable RemoteEvents/Functions. Moving cosmetic traffic off the reliable channel also stops it from queueing ahead of important events. Still reduce the traffic: send at 10-20 Hz or only on meaningful change, quantize angles (buffer/int16), don't echo back to the sender, cull by distance with FireClient to nearby players instead of FireAllClients, and rate-limit and validate per player on the server, because the client controls the send rate.
responses.R6:
Use UnreliableRemoteEvent for high-frequency, cosmetic, superseded-by-the-next-update data: aim direction, look angles, footstep and cosmetic VFX triggers, and continuous positions. Losing or reordering one packet is fine because the next one replaces it. prompt: A developer builds a cross-server lobby browser: every server publishes a ~3 KB JSON table of its players every 5 seconds to one MessagingService topic "ServerList", and every server subscribes to it. The game runs about 500 servers. What limits and behaviours of MessagingService make this design problematic?
answer_key: Each message is limited to about 1 KB (1024 characters), so 3 KB payloads fail; the data must be shrunk or split

Throughput limits scale with players/servers and apply per server, per topic and per game: e.g. sends per server 600 + 240 x players per minute, receives per topic 40 + 80 x servers per minute, receives for the whole game 400 + 200 x servers per minute, subscriptions per server 20 + 8 x players
Delivery is best effort and not guaranteed (callback gets a table with Data and Sent), so a server list built on it can be stale or miss servers; it should tolerate loss

responses.R1: Problems: (1) Message size limit is 1 KB, so a 3 KB payload fails. (2) Publish limit per server is about 150 + 60 x players per minute, and more importantly per-topic delivery limits: each topic can receive roughly 10 + 20 x number of servers messages per minute, and a single subscriber is capped too; 500 servers x 12/min = 6000 publishes/min all fanning out to 500 subscribers (3 million deliveries/min), so it gets throttled and messages are dropped. (3) Delivery is best-effort: no guaranteed delivery, no ordering, no persistence, so a server that subscribes late or misses a message has a stale/incomplete list, and dead servers never 'unpublish' (need TTLs). (4) Each server must hold and parse the whole list (memory/CPU), and subscriptions per server are limited. Better: store each server's entry in a MemoryStore SortedMap/HashMap keyed by JobId with a short expiration (e.g. 30s), refreshed every ~15-30s with a small payload (counts, not full player lists); lobby servers read with GetRangeAsync paginated when the browser is opened. Use MessagingService only for small, rare events (e.g. join requests).
responses.R2:

prompt: A client camera-follow script updates Camera.CFrame in RunService.Heartbeat and the camera visibly jitters. A server projectile script was copied from a client script and uses RunService.RenderStepped, which errors. Which RunService events/methods should each use and why?
answer_key: Camera and other per-frame visual updates should run before the frame renders: RunService.PreRender (supersedes RenderStepped) or RunService:BindToRenderStep with Enum.RenderPriority.Camera; these are client-only

Server per-step logic must use simulation events instead: PreSimulation (supersedes Stepped) before physics or PostSimulation/Heartbeat after physics, scaled by deltaTime, keeping per-frame callbacks light

Client camera: Heartbeat (PostSimulation) fires after physics, out of step with rendering. The default camera script and the character's interpolated position update at a different point in the frame, so your CFrame write lands at an inconsistent time and the camera jitters. Use RunService:BindToRenderStep("FollowCam", Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value + 1, fn), which runs just before rendering and after the default camera (pass the number, not the EnumItem). RenderStepped/PreRender also works for client visuals; unbind with UnbindFromRenderStep. Use dt to smooth (e.g. lerp with 1 - exp(-k*dt)).
Server projectile: RenderStepped/PreRender and BindToRenderStep exist only on the client (the server doesn't render), so they error on the server. Use RunService.Heartbeat (or PostSimulation) for step-after-physics logic, or PreSimulation to set physics state before the step, and use its deltaTime argument so motion is frame-rate independent. Simpler still: compute the trajectory analytically (or use raycasts per step) on the server and let clients render visuals. Summary: client visuals/camera -> render step; server game logic -> Heartbeat/PreSimulation/PostSimulation (or BindToSimulation under Server Authority).

Using the render step with the camera priority runs right before the frame is drawn, using current character positions, so it's smooth. Server projectile: RenderStepped/BindToRenderStep/PreRender exist only on clients (no rendering on the server), hence the error. Use RunService.Heartbeat (PostSimulation) or Stepped/PreSimulation, and move by dt each step (pos += vel * dt), ideally with raycasts between previous and new positions; or use a shared fixed simulation step. Rule: client visuals/camera = render step; server or physics logic = Heartbeat/PreSimulation/PostSimulation.

prompt: A team making a competitive fighting game heard Roblox shipped 'Server Authority' in 2026. How is it turned on, what does it do, and what has to change in their scripts?
answer_key: It is opt-in: set Workspace.AuthorityMode to Server; the server becomes the single source of truth and rejects invalid client movement, while clients predict locally and roll back / resimulate when the server disagrees
Turning it on enables or requires UseFixedSimulation, StreamingEnabled, Deferred SignalBehavior, NextGenerationReplication and PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem (at least three of these named)

Custom gameplay logic must move into RunService:BindToSimulation callbacks and read player input through InputActions so it can be predicted and resimulated; known limits include remote events not being on the shared timeline and a cap of 8 actively playing Animator tracks

responses.R1: Server Authority (2026 beta, then release): enable it on Workspace (AuthorityMode = Server, Workspace.AuthorityMode property / experience setting), which uses fixed-rate physics stepping. What it does: the server owns and simulates all physics, including player characters, so clients lose network-ownership authority. Each client predicts its own character and objects locally with the same input, the server resimulates authoritatively, and clients reconcile and roll back on mismatch. That removes teleport, fly, speed and fling exploits that come from client ownership. Script changes: (1) Movement and ability logic that changes physics must be deterministic and run on both client and server inside RunService:BindToSimulation(fn) at the fixed step, using the provided deltaTime, not RenderStepped/Heartbeat. (2) Read player input through the Input Action System (InputActions replicate to the server for prediction) instead of client-only state or remotes for movement. (3) Remove SetNetworkOwner and client-ownership tricks, and client-side CFrame teleports of the character. (4) Cosmetic effects stay client-side, and hitbox/combat code uses server state (with rewind if needed). Test with network simulation on.
responses.R2:
Turn on: set Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server (full release July 9, 2026; some docs still say beta). It forces NextGenerationReplication, Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem, SignalBehavior = Deferred, StreamingEnabled and UseFixedSimulation.
What it does: the server is authoritative for simulation of characters and physics; clients run predicted simulation from their inputs and the engine resimulates (rollback) when the server disagrees.
